articles.title: Al Jazeera analysis: Iran is offering de-escalation on Hormuz and Yemen at a price others must pay
articles.summary: An Al Jazeera opinion piece argues Iran's offer to ease tensions in the Strait of Hormuz and Yemen comes with conditions -- sanctions relief and an end to the US naval blockade -- that effectively ask Gulf neighbors and Washington to absorb the cost of de-escalation rather than Tehran alone.
articles.body:
As the US-Iran war grinds through its eighth month, an Al Jazeera analysis frames Iran's recent diplomatic posture around a specific structural point: Tehran is offering real de-escalation on two fronts -- reopening the Strait of Hormuz to normal shipping traffic, and reining in the Houthi campaign against Saudi Arabia -- but the price for both is being asked of others, not paid by Iran itself. On Hormuz, Iran's offer to guarantee free navigation is explicitly conditioned on the US easing its naval blockade of Iranian ports and lifting sanctions -- concessions that fall on Washington. On Yemen, Iran's public distancing from the Houthis (its president has repeatedly said "the Houthis are responsible for their own actions" and Iran is "not at war with Saudi Arabia") sidesteps the question of whether Tehran retains real leverage to actually restrain Houthi attacks, rather than just disclaiming responsibility for them after the fact.

This framing matters for reading this week's flurry of diplomatic activity -- the Rubio-Saudi FM talks, Iran's Araghchi meeting Qatari mediators, and reports Iran could reopen Hormuz within seven days if the naval blockade eases -- as genuine offers with real conditions attached, not simply goodwill gestures. The analysis's core argument is that Iran's negotiating position treats de-escalation as a transaction where Washington and its Gulf allies bear the visible cost (lifted sanctions, eased blockade, tolerating continued Iranian influence over armed groups in the region) while Iran retains the underlying capabilities (its nuclear programme, its relationships with regional proxy groups) that created the standoff in the first place.

Whether that reading holds up depends heavily on what specific terms actually get agreed in any real deal -- a genuine, verified Hormuz reopening with reciprocal US concessions would be a substantively different outcome than a temporary lull used to rebuild leverage for the next round of confrontation. For continuity with this newsroom's tracking of the Hormuz/Iran storyline: this analysis adds an important interpretive layer to the purely factual reporting (crude prices, vessel-transit counts, diplomatic meeting readouts) this newsroom has covered all week -- it's a reminder that "de-escalation" headlines don't automatically mean a fair or stable resolution, and the actual terms of any Hormuz agreement matter more than the fact that talks are happening at all.

articles.title: Trump denies offering Iran sanctions relief for nuclear concessions
articles.summary: Trump publicly denied reports that Washington offered Tehran sanctions relief in exchange for nuclear concessions, a denial that lands directly against Iran's own account of ongoing mediated talks and adds fresh uncertainty to whether any US-Iran deal framework actually exists.
articles.body:
Donald Trump denied that the US had offered Iran sanctions relief in exchange for nuclear concessions, according to live coverage of his Monday remarks -- a direct denial of reports describing exactly the kind of trade this newsroom's coverage this week has suggested was on the table (Iran easing its nuclear programme and Hormuz blockade in exchange for sanctions and naval-blockade relief). This denial creates a genuine contradiction worth flagging rather than smoothing over: it's unclear whether Trump is denying that any offer was made at all, denying the specific terms reported, or simply preserving negotiating leverage by publicly disclaiming a position his own negotiators may still be discussing through mediators.

The denial comes the same day Trump told reporters the US will "win" the war with Iran "one way or another" (covered in this newsroom's morning edition) -- a notably harder public posture than the "very good meeting" framing from talks just a week earlier. Taken together, the pattern this week has been consistent: public rhetoric hardening even as private mediated talks reportedly continue, making it genuinely difficult to assess from outside whether a deal is closer or further away than it was days ago.

For continuity purposes, this is worth tracking precisely because it complicates rather than clarifies the storyline: Iranian officials have said they could reopen Hormuz within seven days if the US eases its naval blockade (reported Tuesday), which implies some form of relief-for-concessions framework is genuinely being discussed even if Trump's public denial muddies exactly what shape it takes. The next concrete signal to watch is whether Iran actually moves on Hormuz reopening in the coming days -- if it does, that would suggest real progress behind the public denials; if the current standoff continues unchanged, Trump's denial likely reflects genuine reality rather than negotiating theater.

articles.title: Nifty breaks below its 200-week moving average for the first time since Covid
articles.summary: The Nifty 50 cracked below its 200-week moving average -- a level it has held since the pandemic crash -- as crude near $107 and rising bond yields extend the market's slide, a technical breach analysts flag as a meaningful signal distinct from the week's day-to-day volatility.
articles.body:
The Nifty 50 index broke below its 200-week moving average for the first time since the Covid-19 crash, a technical threshold that market analysts treat as a meaningfully different signal than ordinary daily volatility -- a 200-week average smooths out roughly four years of trading, so a breach below it typically reflects a genuine shift in longer-term trend sentiment rather than short-term noise around a single news event.

This lands directly on top of the trend this newsroom has tracked all week: crude near $107 a barrel on the escalating US-Iran and Saudi-Houthi fronts, the rupee breaching 96 per dollar, and now a market-structure signal suggesting the pressure has built up enough to break a level that survived every other selloff since the pandemic. The distinction matters for anyone deciding how to read this week's declines: a single bad session is noise, but a 200-week moving average breach is the kind of technical signal that shows up in institutional risk models and can trigger further selling from funds with rules-based exposure limits, independent of what happens with the underlying Iran/Hormuz news flow.

For continuity: this is the technical confirmation of a pattern this newsroom has been narrating qualitatively since Tuesday morning's edition (four consecutive sessions of crude-driven pressure) -- what was previously described in terms of daily point-drops and percentage moves has now crossed into genuine longer-term-trend territory. Whether this proves to be the low point of the current selloff or an early signal of a deeper correction depends heavily on the same Iran/Hormuz diplomatic threads covered elsewhere in this edition -- a credible de-escalation would be the most likely catalyst for markets to recover back above this level, while continued escalation would likely extend the breach further.

articles.title: RBI drains $20 billion via FX operations to defend the rupee
articles.summary: The Reserve Bank of India pulled roughly $20 billion of liquidity out of the banking system through foreign-exchange operations aimed at supporting the rupee, a move with direct knock-on effects for domestic interest rates and banking-system liquidity just as the currency struggles near record lows.
articles.body:
The RBI has drained approximately $20 billion in liquidity through foreign-exchange operations, an intervention aimed at supporting the rupee as it struggles near the 96-per-dollar level flagged in this newsroom's Tuesday morning coverage. The mechanism is direct: when the RBI sells dollars from its reserves to buy rupees (defending the currency from further depreciation), it simultaneously pulls rupee liquidity out of the banking system as a side effect -- the same intervention that props up the currency also tightens domestic money-market conditions.

That liquidity-tightening effect has real consequences for interest rates independent of any formal RBI rate decision: draining $20 billion from the banking system pushes short-term money-market rates higher mechanically, even without the RBI raising its policy repo rate at all. This connects directly to the other RBI story in this edition -- Nomura's prediction that actual policy rate hikes will be far more modest (50 basis points) than the market's current pricing (125 basis points) -- because FX-driven liquidity tightening can partially substitute for formal rate hikes in cooling inflation and supporting the currency, reducing the RBI's need to move its headline policy rate as aggressively as the market currently expects.

The scale here -- $20 billion is a substantial single intervention -- signals the RBI is treating the rupee's recent slide as serious enough to warrant direct, sizeable action rather than just verbal guidance (like Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta's "has scope to stabilise, appreciate" comments from last week's edition). For anyone tracking the rupee/rate story across this week's coverage: this is the concrete operational follow-through on the currency-support commitments RBI officials have been signaling verbally, and it directly informs how much room the RBI actually has to raise rates further without over-tightening an already liquidity-constrained banking system.

articles.title: Nomura predicts RBI will hike just 50bps versus market's 125bps bet
articles.summary: Nomura forecasts the RBI will raise rates by only 50 basis points this cycle, well below the market's 125 basis-point pricing, anticipating inflation pressures will moderate faster than currently expected -- a materially different read from the more hawkish agency forecasts flagged earlier this week.
articles.body:
Nomura is forecasting the RBI will raise its policy rate by just 50 basis points in the current cycle -- less than half of what markets are currently pricing in at 125 basis points. The bank's reasoning centers on an expectation that inflation pressures will moderate faster than the consensus view assumes, a materially more dovish read than the picture painted by the OECD/ADB/S&P/Fitch forecast cluster this newsroom covered Thursday, several of which explicitly flagged rising inflation (driven by elevated oil prices and food costs) as justifying a rate-hike cycle.

This creates a genuine, trackable disagreement between forecasters worth watching resolve: if Nomura is right and the RBI hikes only 50bps, that would represent a meaningfully looser policy stance than markets currently expect -- generally supportive for equities and growth, though potentially less supportive for the rupee than a more aggressive hike would be. If the market's 125bps pricing proves closer to reality, that implies inflation concerns (from the same $107 crude and Iran-war-driven cost pressures flagged throughout this edition) are more persistent than Nomura's forecast assumes.

Read alongside the RBI's $20 billion FX-liquidity drain (covered above), there's a plausible reconciling story: if FX intervention is already doing some of the currency-defense and liquidity-tightening work that a rate hike would otherwise need to do, that gives the RBI room to hike less aggressively on the headline policy rate than the market currently expects -- exactly the outcome Nomura is forecasting. Whether that read holds will become clear at the RBI's next Monetary Policy Committee meeting, the concrete event to watch against both Nomura's 50bps call and the market's more hawkish 125bps pricing.

articles.title: Jaishankar: a trade agreement can improve India-US ties as Goyal holds Washington talks
articles.summary: External Affairs Minister Jaishankar said a finalised trade agreement could strengthen India-US relations as Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal begins his week of Washington trade talks, framing the deal as a relationship-building tool rather than just a tariff-reduction exercise.
articles.body:
External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said a trade agreement between India and the US "can contribute to better" bilateral ties, timed to coincide with Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal's arrival in Washington for the week-long trade talks this newsroom covered in Tuesday's morning edition. Jaishankar's framing is notable for positioning the deal as a relationship-strengthening instrument in its own right, not simply a tariff-and-market-access negotiation -- a framing that puts diplomatic weight behind Goyal's own "done and dusted" characterization from last week.

This is the clearest signal yet that India's trade and foreign-policy apparatus are speaking with one voice on the US relationship, at a moment when the two departments' priorities could plausibly diverge -- Commerce wants market access and favorable tariff terms, while External Affairs manages the broader relationship including the Russian-oil sanctions pressure (covered in Tuesday's edition) and defense/strategic cooperation. Jaishankar explicitly linking the trade deal to overall relationship quality suggests New Delhi is treating the BTA negotiation as strategically important beyond its direct economic terms.

For continuity: this adds a foreign-policy dimension to the trade-deal storyline this newsroom has tracked through Goyal's own comments (Thursday: "done and dusted"; Tuesday morning: departure for US visit amid Russian-crude complications). Watch for whether Jaishankar's own diplomatic engagements during Goyal's Washington week produce any parallel announcements -- historically, major India-US trade milestones have been accompanied by coordinated messaging from both the Commerce and External Affairs ministries, and this statement is an early instance of that pattern for the current negotiation round.

articles.title: The trade irony behind Trump's Russia-oil threat: Russia is now buying its own oil back as fuel from India
articles.summary: As Washington threatens 100% tariffs on buyers of Russian crude, Indian refiners are exporting refined fuel products made from that same Russian crude back to Russia itself -- a byproduct of India's refining capacity that complicates the simple narrative of who benefits from India's Russian-oil purchases.
articles.body:
A genuinely counterintuitive wrinkle in the India-Russia-US oil triangle this newsroom has tracked all week: Indian refiners, who buy discounted Russian crude oil and refine it into finished fuel products, are in some cases selling refined fuel back to Russia itself -- meaning Russia is effectively buying back its own crude, now processed into higher-value refined product, from Indian refiners. This complicates the straightforward narrative underlying the US tariff threat (that India buying Russian crude directly funds Russia's war effort) by showing the actual trade flows are more circular than a simple crude-oil-purchase framing suggests.

The mechanism reflects India's refining-capacity advantage: Indian refiners have significant spare capacity and specialized equipment for processing the type of heavy, sour crude Russia exports (much of which Western refiners have stopped buying due to sanctions), letting India import discounted Russian crude, refine it domestically, and re-export the finished products -- diesel, jet fuel, and other refined outputs -- to whichever markets will buy them, including in some cases markets connected back to Russia's own fuel needs. This is a legitimate, well-established pattern in global refining economics (buying cheap crude and adding value through refining is exactly what refiners are supposed to do), but it does sharpen the question of exactly what the US tariff threat (tied to the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, covered in Tuesday's edition) is actually meant to interrupt.

For India's negotiating position ahead of Goyal's Washington trade talks this week: this story is a useful data point that the crude-oil-purchase issue is more nuanced than a simple "India funds Russia" framing, since a meaningful share of the value India adds through refining doesn't straightforwardly translate into Russian war-financing the way a direct crude purchase might. Whether US negotiators find this distinction persuasive, or continue treating any Russian-crude-linked trade as equally problematic, will likely shape how much room India actually has to continue current import levels (already declining to a five-month low of 1.75 million barrels per day, per Tuesday's coverage) without further escalating the tariff threat.

articles.title: AI agent security startup Reco raises $55M as the safety-tooling market gets crowded
articles.summary: AI agent security startup Reco raised $55 million as investor interest in agent-governance tooling surges following this week's Nvidia platform launch and the Hugging Face/Medicare breach incidents -- a concrete sign the AI-safety debate is now also a fast-growing investment category, not just a policy conversation.
articles.body:
Reco, a startup building security tooling for AI agents, raised $55 million as investor interest floods into the AI-agent-security category -- directly following this newsroom's coverage of Nvidia's own Open Agent Safety Platform launch and the Hugging Face and Australian Medicare breaches that have driven the week's broader AI-safety-debate storyline. TechCrunch's framing is notable: AI agent security startups are now "crowding the market," meaning Reco isn't a first-mover capitalizing on an obscure niche but one of several well-funded competitors racing to solve the same governance problem Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic have all separately confirmed is real this week.

This is the clearest evidence yet that the AI-safety debate this newsroom has tracked -- spanning Anthropic's IPO-filing risk warnings, OpenAI's cancelled model release, and Nvidia's kill-switch product -- has created a genuine, fundable market category rather than staying a purely academic or regulatory conversation. Where Nvidia's product targets large frontier labs directly evaluating their own models, a wave of startups like Reco building adjacent tooling suggests enterprise customers deploying third-party AI agents (not just the labs building the underlying models) now see agent governance as a purchasable necessity rather than a problem only the largest AI companies need to solve.

For anyone tracking where AI-related venture capital is flowing amid this week's broader funding news (AMD's $8.2 billion World Labs acquisition, EliseAI's $4 billion valuation, SiMa.ai's $150 million raise, all covered in recent editions): AI-agent security is emerging as a distinct, well-capitalized sub-category within the broader AI investment boom, directly caused by the same incidents that have made this week's AI-safety headlines -- a case where the underlying risk itself is generating the investment thesis for the companies trying to mitigate it.

articles.title: Taiwan's US arms pipeline slows as F-16 and T-Dome deals face delays
articles.summary: Deliveries under Taiwan's $14 billion US arms package -- including Lockheed Martin F-16 fighter jets and the T-Dome missile-defense system -- are running behind schedule, raising questions about US commitment to Taiwan's defense buildup even as tensions with China stay elevated.
articles.body:
Taiwan's pipeline of US arms deliveries is slowing, with the island's roughly $14 billion package of Lockheed Martin F-16 fighter jets and the T-Dome missile-defense system both facing delays, according to Mint's compilation of available reporting. The specifics of the delays aren't fully public, but the pattern itself is significant: Taiwan has treated rapid US arms deliveries as a core pillar of its defense posture against China, and any visible slowdown raises questions -- inside Taiwan and among regional observers -- about how firmly committed Washington actually is to the pace of Taiwan's defense buildup, independent of public statements of support.

The timing connects directly to this week's broader US-China dynamic: Xi Jinping's Washington summit and his "Thucydides Trap can be overcome" remarks (covered in Thursday's edition) explicitly named Taiwan as one of the unresolved friction points between the two powers, alongside trade and AI regulation. A slowing arms pipeline to Taiwan, arriving the same week as a notably warmer US-China summit tone, is the kind of concrete signal that could be read either as coincidental scheduling friction or as a substantive (if unstated) US concession to Beijing as part of the broader effort to "cool the temperature" on multiple fronts simultaneously (the same framing China's Middle East envoy used regarding the Iran war, also covered this week).

For anyone tracking the US-China-Taiwan dynamic alongside this newsroom's other geopolitical coverage this week: the genuinely open question is whether this arms-pipeline slowdown is a logistics and manufacturing-capacity issue (plausible, given how stretched US defense production has been across multiple simultaneous conflicts and commitments) or a deliberate signal tied to the broader US-China de-escalation effort. Taiwan's own government response, and whether Washington offers any public explanation or accelerated timeline, are the concrete things to watch next.

articles.title: Meta launches Muse for Small Business, taking its enterprise AI push at 200 million businesses on Facebook
articles.summary: Meta unveiled Muse for Small Business, connecting its AI agent to Asana, Zoom, Intuit, Canva and Slack plus Meta's own ad and social accounts, arriving the same day OpenAI holds its developer conference as Zuckerberg pushes Muse -- which reportedly surpassed ChatGPT on Apple's App Store this month -- beyond consumer use into a direct challenge to OpenAI and Anthropic's enterprise ambitions.
articles.body:
Meta launched Muse for Small Business, connecting its AI agent to popular small-business software including Asana, Zoom, Intuit, Box, Canva and Salesforce's Slack, plus Meta's own ad accounts and professional Instagram and Facebook profiles. The company didn't disclose pricing beyond noting the existing consumer Muse app is free with usage limits and subscription-based beyond that. The launch lands the same day OpenAI is holding its own developer conference (covered in this newsroom's earlier editions), a scheduling overlap that reads as a deliberate competitive signal rather than coincidence.

This follows Meta's Monday announcement of a new enterprise platform -- for which it poached MongoDB CEO CJ Desai -- that will bundle a Muse agent, a separate business agent, and a coding tool. Taken together with Tuesday's small-business launch, Meta is moving fast to build out enterprise AI infrastructure just weeks after Muse's consumer debut: the app reportedly shot to the top of Apple's App Store on September 8, surpassing ChatGPT, with Evercore analyst Mark Mahaney projecting it could reach 100 million users within six to twelve months.

Zuckerberg's framing at last week's Meta Connect -- calling Muse "the centerpiece" of his AI strategy -- underscores how central this bet has become for a company long dependent on digital advertising for nearly all its revenue. Meta already has real distribution advantage for the small-business push specifically: the company says 200 million small businesses already operate on Facebook, giving Muse for Small Business a built-in user base Meta doesn't need to acquire from scratch, unlike OpenAI or Anthropic's enterprise products.

For anyone tracking this week's broader AI-industry-structure storyline (Anthropic's IPO filing, OpenAI's cancelled model release, AMD's World Labs acquisition, Nvidia's agent-security platform, Reco's funding round): Meta's enterprise push is a reminder that the AI-safety and AI-infrastructure stories dominating this week's coverage are happening alongside, not instead of, an intense and separate competitive race for enterprise AI market share -- Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic are all fighting for the same corporate customers even as they separately navigate safety scrutiny, IPO preparations and agent-security incidents.

articles.title: Nvidia authorises $150 billion more in buybacks as Huang calls the stock 'misunderstood'
articles.summary: Nvidia added $150 billion to its share-repurchase programme on top of May's $80 billion plan, with its forward P/E ratio at its cheapest level in a decade despite analysts projecting 60% net income growth to $385 billion in fiscal 2028 -- CEO Jensen Huang calling Nvidia 'the world's first and only growth value stock.'
articles.body:
Nvidia authorised an additional $150 billion for share buybacks, on top of an $80 billion repurchase plan from May (when it also raised its quarterly dividend from 1 cent to 25 cents per share). The move comes as Nvidia's fiscal 2028 price-to-earnings ratio sits at just 14.5 -- its cheapest valuation multiple in a decade, and below every megacap peer except Micron -- even as analysts project net income near $385 billion for that year, up 60% year-over-year and more than fivefold over three years. CEO Jensen Huang had previewed the logic last month, telling CNBC's Jim Cramer "buying back Nvidia stock is a tremendous opportunity."

The valuation gap is the real story here: Nvidia, now worth over $5.5 trillion, trades at less than a quarter of its five-year average P/E of 62.9, despite its own guidance (given to investors in August) projecting 70% sales growth in fiscal 2028 -- implying hundreds of billions of dollars more in sales than Wall Street had previously modeled. Huang addressed the disconnect directly at a Goldman Sachs conference this month, calling Nvidia "misunderstood" and arguing it should be valued for both its growth rate and its future-earnings profile simultaneously: "we are the world's first and only growth value stock... people are trying to figure out which one we are. We are both."

Analysts offered competing explanations for the compressed multiple. Deepwater Asset Management's Gene Munster said investors are worried growth simply can't continue at recent rates: "it's just really hard for investors to get comfortable that that's going to continue." Melius Research's Ben Reitzes took the opposite view, saying the stock "deserves to be higher given its growth rate" and that the expanded buyback program itself should help close the valuation gap. UBS estimated the stepped-up repurchases could add 8 cents per share to calendar-year 2027 earnings (estimated at $17.16), while Nvidia's own share count could shrink by 4% if it deploys the full new authorization.

For context against rivals: Nvidia's fiscal 2028 P/E trails Apple (35.5), Alphabet (22.6), Microsoft (21.7) and Amazon (23.2), and even its direct AI-chip competitors Broadcom (18.2), AMD (38.2) and Intel (54.7) -- notably, none of those rivals are forecasting anywhere close to Nvidia's projected 70% sales growth, which is exactly the disconnect Huang and bullish analysts are pointing to as justification for the buyback. The announcement came alongside Nvidia's own new agent-security software (covered in this newsroom's earlier coverage of the Open Agent Safety Platform), and the stock rose almost 2% on the combined news Monday.

articles.title: Supreme Court calls 10x cancer-drug price markups 'carnage', questions why retailers profit while patients pay
articles.summary: The Supreme Court questioned why an essential cancer drug supplied to retailers for ₹3,000 sells to consumers for ₹27,000, with the Centre's Solicitor General conceding private hospitals -- not drugmakers -- pocket most of the markup, as the court weighs applying DPCO's 16% retailer-margin cap uniformly across essential medicines.
articles.body:
The Supreme Court expressed sharp concern over the pricing gap between what retailers pay for essential medicines and what consumers are charged, with a Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta calling the disparity "carnage" that ultimately burdens taxpayers. Justice Mehta highlighted a specific, stark example: an essential cancer drug supplied to retailers for around ₹3,000 sold to consumers for ₹27,000 -- a nearly tenfold markup -- and directly asked "where does this chunk of money go?"

The court is weighing whether to extend the Drugs (Prices Control) Order (DPCO) 2013's 16% retailer-margin cap uniformly across all essential medicines, rather than the current system where that cap applies unevenly. Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, representing the Centre, made a notable concession under questioning: "the pharma company is not the gainer. The gainer is the private hospital" -- directly identifying private hospitals, not drug manufacturers, as the primary beneficiary of the inflated pricing. The Bench separately flagged the common practice of private hospitals requiring patients to buy medicines from in-house pharmacies, eliminating any ability to shop for lower prices elsewhere even when identical drugs are available cheaper.

The taxpayer-burden angle the court raised has a direct fiscal dimension: when patients receive treatment through government-funded schemes like Ayushman Bharat, inflated drug prices mean taxpayers -- not just individual patients -- absorb the cost of the markup. "The government doesn't pay, the taxpayer pays. This affects a larger section of society," the Bench observed. This isn't the court's first strong language on the issue: it had previously described the same price-to-retailer versus MRP gap as "dacoity," remarking "if this is not extortion, then what is it? People sell their houses, ornaments to get treatment."

The Solicitor General asked for time to present the government's existing drug-pricing mechanisms in detail, with the matter now posted for further hearing on October 12, 2026 -- giving the Centre roughly two weeks to formulate a substantive response to the Bench's direct questioning about extending the uniform margin cap. The underlying petitions, filed by advocate Kishan Chand Jain and paediatric surgeon Sanjay Kulshrestha, seek broader court intervention to regulate prices across drugs, medical equipment and generic medicines -- meaning whatever framework emerges from the October 12 hearing could have implications well beyond the cancer-drug example that prompted Tuesday's sharpest exchanges.

briefs.text: Iran's rial hit a fresh record low of 2.5 million to the dollar as mediators push for a US truce and Strait of Hormuz reopening. The currency collapse underscores the economic pressure driving Tehran's stated openness to reopening Hormuz within seven days if the US naval blockade eases.

The Indian government is exploring alternate air routes via China and Bhutan to cut costs from the extended Pakistan airspace ban, which has raised operating expenses for Air India, IndiGo and SpiceJet. The move comes as elevated crude prices add further financial pressure on carriers already absorbing longer flight times.

Enterprise AI startup EliseAI was valued at $4 billion in its latest funding round, led by Andreessen Horowitz and Bessemer Venture Partners with participation from Ontario Teachers' Pension Plan, Sapphire Ventures and Navitas Capital. It's another large AI funding round in a week already featuring AMD's World Labs deal and Reco's agent-security raise.

AceVector, the parent company of Snapdeal and Unicommerce, saw its IPO subscribed nearly 5 times on the final day of bidding. The offering adds to this week's busy Indian IPO calendar alongside NSE's own recent listing.
